Our study aims to bridge this knowledge gap by examining the effectiveness of activities in the ICML Automated Cup and the FIFA World Cup, with an emphasis on the relationship between player performance and activity performance. Our analysis reveals that there are distinct differences in the effectiveness of activities across these two competitions. Furthermore, we identify the key activities that have the most significant impact on the outcome of the FIFA World Cup, and we also explore the potential applications of our findings, such as the use of predictive models to forecast player performance.

A cutting-edge terahertz measurement technique has been developed to study
the dielectric properties of complex liquids with significant dielectric loss.
The innovative setup consists of two high-speed silicon transistors that
convert the dielectric properties of a sample into voltage fluctuations.
By analyzing the interference patterns between the two transisters, the
system can measure the dielectric properties of the sample without being
physically in contact with it. The system's functionality is verified using
standard silicon water solutions at various temperatures. The system's results
are consistent with the results obtained from conventional microwave tests,
showing promise in the potential to expand the measurement range even further.
The new system enables precise analysis of the dielectric properties of the
sample at frequencies that were previously inaccessible, offering a wide range
of applications in biochemistry, pharmaceuticals, agriculture, and environmental
sciences.

The COVID-19 pandemic has presented humanity with an unprecedented health crisis, with widespread infections and deaths. In an effort to combat the virus, multiple strategies have been proposed, with varying degrees of impact. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has proven to be a highly effective tool in analyzing large datasets, with numerous applications in healthcare, transportation, and other fields. Given the urgent need to combat COVID-19, this study aims to leverage AI capabilities to analyze large datasets, with a proposed framework for a data-centric approach. The framework is composed of three key components: data collection, data analysis, and decision-making, with a focus on accurate decision-making to mitigate the pandemic's effects.

In this paper, a multi-phase, fluid interaction system is examined using a multi-phase, meshless approach. The Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics method is employed to model the fluid phase, and a finite element method is utilized to model the rigid body. The interaction between the fluid and rigid body is taken into account through a coupling strategy. The integration of the finite element and particle fields is facilitated by a mapping technique. The effectiveness of the proposed framework is demonstrated in a series of numerical studies, including a comparison of results with existing literature and an investigation of the impact of the interfacial zone's size.

Nodal materials, characterized by zero energy gaps in momentum space, have garnered significant attention due to their unique properties and diverse applications in solid-state physics. These materials' response to external conditions, including light and magnetic fields, can be influenced by the topology of nodal surfaces, resulting in novel physical phenomena. This review focuses on the topological properties of nodal surfaces in nodal crystals, providing an overview of standard models and recent implementations in experimental platforms. We also discuss emerging methods for identifying new nodal surface structures in high-dimensional spaces and outline the distinct signatures of nodal surfaces in various measurements.

The HL-LHC's high event rate requires advanced simulation techniques to produce reliable data for the experimenters. Event generators play a vital role in this process by providing pre-calculated results which are then tailored to specific experiments. With the advancement of Monte Carlo simulations and the emergence of new physics models, event generator development has become a priority. This document outlines the shared software development process for Wajehm and GMENPHO event generators, highlighting their use of new physics models and highlighting challenges such as handling massive event samples and ensuring the integrity of the simulation output.

We introduce a novel invariant characteristic, and we prove it's a full invariant for full-area subshifts of finite type under the condition that the average return times have a common divisor. This divergence from the established maximal average return time property arises from a fundamental difference in how these invariants are defined - one based on a count of return events and the other on a measure of their area.

The formation of massive stars and compact star clusters is a widespread phenomenon in the spiral arms of the Milky Way, but it is also observed in the outer galaxy. The outer galaxy is characterized by a unique environment with less gas and dust, and a lower rate of star formation. Despite this, some areas in the outer galaxy exhibit characteristics of the birthplaces of massive stars, such as the formation of H II regions and dust continuum sources. The origin of the gas and dust within these regions is still unclear. This study used the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array to examine the CO and C18O emission in the G32.97+0.18 giant molecular cloud, and found evidence that a large amount of dark molecular matter is present. The presence of this matter is evident in the CO and C18O emission, and is consistent with the distribution of dust emission. The properties of the cloud suggest that a large population of massive stars is formed through the collapse of the cloud due to the gravitational force. The cloud's high column density and high gravitational free-fall time indicate that it is likely the remnant of a large molecular cloud that has undergone disruption due to the galaxy's spiral arm.

This research develops a mathematical model to analyze the strategic interactions between employers and employees in a restricted labor market. Employing game theory and differential equations, the model captures the dynamic employment decisions made by both parties, with the employees' choices influenced by a fixed maximum work hours constraint. In contrast to previous models that assumed infinite hours, the finite hours constraint introduced in this study leads to distinct outcomes, even at high levels of productivity. Specifically, this model reveals that as the productivity level increases, the number of employed workers grows more rapidly than the available work hours. Furthermore, this model examines the impact of varying employee numbers on the distribution of work hours, revealing an asymptotic normal distribution in the labor market's limit.

Our investigation focuses on the behavior of an active polar suspension with varying particle size, examining how hydrodynamic interactions affect active particles with multiple flocks and individual entities. Through the integration of a stochastic differential equation into a computational model, we capture the intricate dynamics of complex particle clusters and unclustered particles. Utilizing advanced computational methods, we provide an in-depth analysis of the dynamic interactions within and between these particles and the collective patterns that emerge. Our findings indicate that the presence of multiple flocks leads to a significant reduction in the diffusion rate of individual particles and a significant reduction in the movement of unclustered particles caused by unclustered particles. Conversely, unclustered particles experience reduced movement due to flocked particles and a decrease in the emergence of collective patterns due to the increased size of active particles.

Within the framework of the heavy quark limit and the pion pseudovector channel, 
we've employed the bag model and the modified pouch model to calculate the form factors 
for doubly charmed baryon decay. Our analysis reveals that the pouch model offers greater 
treatment of the non-perturbative phenomena in comparison to the standard bag model. 
We have also derived the form factors for all possible decay modes of the singly heavy 
baryons $X(4660)$ and $X(4630)$, which originate from the doubly charmed baryon $\Xi_c^{++}$ 
and $\Xi_c^{+}$. Our results indicate that the pouch model yields more favorable outcomes 
for the transition form factors compared to the bag model, particularly at large $q^2$.

This study introduces a novel task, using embodied conversations for self-localization in an indoor environment. The key challenge lies in distinguishing between rooms, a task often previously tackled with various degrees of external assistance. In contrast, our proposed method relies solely on external guidance in the form of a caller asking for the subject's location, without any additional information. A key innovation is the use of 2D map navigation, as opposed to 3D self-positioning, and the development of a learning framework that integrates 2D map reconstruction, self-location, and embodied conversation. The framework is trained end-to-end and tested on the NavGraph dataset, achieving commendable results with a mean absolute error of 1.58m and 2.30m when utilizing 2D and 3D maps respectively.

This study introduces the Band Significance Factor (BSF) approach, which is a tool-independent, semi-automatic method for selecting the most critical frequency bands in signal processing applications, particularly suitable for monitoring rotating equipment. The proposed method is based on analyzing time-domain signals using Fast Fourier Transformation (FFT) to identify key frequency bands. A comprehensive database of simulated and experimental signals was developed to test the BSF method, which demonstrated its effectiveness in selecting the most informative frequency bands for fault identification in rotating machinery. In comparison to the traditional method using FFT, BSF showed a higher level of effectiveness in detecting the most critical frequency bands for fault detection, as evidenced by its application in monitoring the health of gear, bearing, and rotor systems under various operating conditions.

We conducted an in-depth analysis of the superconducting state in CaIrSi3 and CaPtSi3 through the application of muon spectroscopy in a magnetic field, in conjunction with critical field measurements. Our results indicate that both compounds have an extended base state, contrary to previously proposed nodeless models. In contrast, our findings are more in line with a more intricate electronic structure, as supported by the material's Fermi surface topology. In the case of CaIrSi3, a d-wave base state is suggested by the observed field dependence. In the case of CaPtSi3, a base state with a more intricate electronic structure cannot be accurately determined from the obtained data, but is likely to be a d-wave base state.

This letter introduces the Sparse Grid Attributes method for efficiently handling high-dimensional optimal control problems with a focus on reducing the computational burden of solving the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation. By utilizing a grid-based approximation and adaptive sampling, the method enables the creation of lower-dimensional, piecewise constant functions that accurately represent high-dimensional value functions within the problem's feasible region. Effective implementation of the method necessitates a value function-based feedback control strategy, and we provide a theoretical justification for its performance and stability. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulations of an optimal water reservoir control problem.

The assessment of quantum machine learning models using quantum data is a critical component of the Machine Learning benchmarking process. This study delves into the potential of quantum machine learning to address a real-world problem in human assessment by developing a classification model to determine the grades of quantum exams taken by students. Our analysis focuses on the effectiveness of binary classification of quantum exams in various formats, including binary, ternary, and quaternary, and evaluates the accuracy of these assessments. Notably, our experiment reveals that binary grading is a viable option for evaluating quantum exams, producing accurate results with a low error rate, while offering the advantage of being more resistant to noise and easier to implement compared to ternary and quaternary grading.

The goal of the paper is to highlight the significance of the link between the modeling of dynamic interactions within complex multi-energy systems and the effectiveness of the regulation in place, specifically in achieving a low-carbon transition. To accomplish this, the paper proposes a basic framework that illustrates how energy production, transportation, and consumption within interconnected multi-energy systems can be interconnected, resulting in linear dependence on the level of the system. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates how the complexity of the system's dynamics can be influenced by the system's level, which in turn affects the ability of the regulator to implement policies aimed at achieving a low-carbon transition. Specifically, the paper examines the impact of the system's level on the existence and uniqueness of the equilibrium point, as well as its stability in the face of policy disturbances. Lastly, the paper presents a basic model that illustrates the link between system level and climate change mitigation through the use of a tax or price signal, which is applied to a system with various sectors and technologies.

The 2D filtration process is modeled by the 2D diffusion equation, representing real-world phenomena such as heat and mass transfer, whose solution requires advanced computational techniques for accurate and efficient results. To address this need, this study proposes a novel approach that uses a feedforward neural network to approximate the solution of the 2D filtration problem, eliminating the need for a grid to discretize the domain. Building on the insights from previous work by the same authors, this method leverages the potential theory of positive harmonic functions to ensure the accuracy of the neural network's output. To demonstrate its effectiveness, this approach will be applied to a 2D Poisson problem, before being generalized to more complex 2D filtration problems, including those with non-homogeneous material properties and with boundaries subject to Neumann boundary conditions.

We utilized rapid MRI to conduct a detailed study of heat transfer within a packed bed of superparamagnetic particles, achieving the first-ever mapping of both temperature and gas-phase magnetization in this setup. Initially, the particle mixture was heated to elevate the fluid phase temperature and then allowed to reach a steady state before being imaged. Our findings revealed a linear correlation between gas-phase magnetization and fluid-phase temperature across various parameters, such as fluid phase temperature, gas mean velocity, and pore size. This relationship can be leveraged to calculate the gas-phase temperature using a rapid MRI scan, which requires a minimal timeframe of under a second. Moreover, our research demonstrated that the rate of heat transfer in the bed is directly proportional to the square of the gas mean velocity, adhering to a fundamental principle of heat transfer. This study marks the first-ever measurement of heat distribution within a packed bed through MRI technology.

In superconductors with strong magnetic interactions, the mechanism of dynamic or quantum fluctuations plays a significant role in their behavior. The interplay between these quantum fluctuations and other factors, such as disorder and thermal influences, can result in a complex pattern of phase transitions that may exhibit non-traditional features under varying levels of cooling. The compound UTe$_2$ serves as an ideal test case for our theoretical framework, as it exhibits a rich phase diagram influenced by magnetic fields and temperatures. Our analysis reveals that the observed superconducting phase diagram is a direct outcome of the interplay between two distinct temperature ranges, along with the disorder and thermal fluctuations present within the system. The effective temperature at which superconductivity emerges is reduced as the quantum fluctuations increase, ultimately leading to the formation of a reentrant superconducting phase at certain levels of disorder and temperatures above a specific threshold. The reentrance of the superconducting phase in the UTe$_2$ compound is attributed to the unique characteristics of its two-site exchange interaction, which is a result of the interplay between its magnetic and superconducting properties.

This research paper presents a method for automatically adjusting the transmitter settings in an
UWB chip during operation, leading to improved communication stability. By leveraging
reinforcement learning, we've created an agent that makes adjustments in response to a reward signal,
allowing for seamless integration into existing chips with minimal modifications. Through testing on
real UWB devices, we've found that our approach yields a significant reduction in 2-way communication
errors, outperforming a fixed configuration approach.

We examine the k-median clustering problem in a graph setting, where we consider two specific distance metrics: the Hausdorff distance in graph theory and the discrete Fr\'{e}chet distance in computational geometry. In computational geometry, the discrete Fr\'{e}cher distance measures the minimum alignment required between two graphs, while the Hausdorff distance in graph theory is defined as the minimum combined distance between vertices of one graph and a set of matched vertices in another graph. By applying the metric of the Johnson-Lindenstrauss convex body, we obtain upper bounds for the k-median grouping problem under these two distance metrics. Additionally, we prove the tightness of these bounds through a reduction to a lower bound for the k-median clustering problem.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MRL) presents a complex problem due to agents' interdependencies, which are often modeled using mixed actions. This complicates the application of single-agent reinforcement learning methods, as they do not account for interdependencies among agents. By treating MRL as a decentralized optimization problem, we apply Double Averaging Primal-Dual (DAPD) optimization to develop the first time-consistent, non-asymptotic MRL algorithm based on average reward, the first of its kind in the literature. Our method works for both finite and countably state-action spaces, and is particularly robust in countably scenarios where existing non-asymptotic MRL methods struggle to produce consistent results.

We investigate the coalgebraic structure inherent in the proof systems for the quantified harmonic $\mu$-calculus, a universal modal $\mu$-logic with harmonic modalities that can express reachability and distance relationships, as well as its sublogic, the harmonic LTL. The harmonic $\mu$-calculus is shown to be coalgebraic, with its coalgebraic semantics defined through a bimorphism semantics that can be derived from its standard semantics through a logical translation. Furthermore, we establish that the harmonic LTL has a complete decidable model checking mechanism for a broad class of complex state spaces, with model checking for both the harmonic $\mu$-calculus itself being reducible to that of LTL. Additionally, we also prove coalgebraic soundness and completeness for a validity checking algorithm based on a new characterization of the harmonic $\mu$-calculus, as well as its sublogic, as fixed point theories.

Reconstructing the initial conditions of nonlinear partial differential equations from partial observations is a complex task. When dealing with high-dimensional data, traditional methods struggle to accommodate the curse of dimensionality, and grid-based approaches can result in massive datasets that overwhelm modern computing systems. In this paper, we propose a versatile solution to this problem, combining low-rank tensor decomposition with Isogeometric Galerkin methods to efficiently recover sparse high-dimensional initial conditions from random data. The proposed approach is independent of specific PDEs, making it a universal method, and is demonstrated on a wave equation problem in 2D with Isogeometric Analysis.

This research introduces an innovative method for creating detailed air quality maps with high spatial resolution, while minimizing the cost of the sensor infrastructure. The proposed approach employs regression-based techniques to integrate data from existing sensor networks with lower spatial resolution. By leveraging the geographical information provided by GPS data from vehicles and combined with information about road layouts and sensor locations, the method can accurately estimate air quality at unsampled locations. The presented framework is capable of generating hourly air quality maps for a large metropolitan area with significantly reduced computational overhead. Comprehensive experiments using both simulated and real-world data demonstrate the method's effectiveness in creating detailed air quality maps with high spatial resolution, outperforming comparable techniques in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency.

Consider a finite field $\mathbf{F}$ of order $q$ where $q$ is an odd power of a prime and let $I$ represent a second-class involution of $\mathbf{F}^*$ with the property that $I^2 = 1$.  A group $G$ is defined over the ring $\mathbf{K} = \mathbb{F}_q[X]/(X^q-I)$ with the structure of the semidirect product of $G_0$, a split extension of the finite abelian group $A$ by the field $\mathbf{K}^*$ through a non-trivial $\mathbf{K}$-linear automorphism $\varphi$.  The problem is to find a Weil representation $\rho$ of $G$ over the ring $\mathbf{K}$.  The existence of $\rho$ is guaranteed by the construction of a non-trivial element $u\in\mathbf{K}^*$ such that $u^2I$ is an element of $\mathbf{K}^*$.  The element $u$ is constructed by first finding a non-trivial element $a\in\mathbf{F}^*$ such that $a^2I(a) = 1$.  The element $u$ is then defined as the product of $a$ with an element of the form $1+x$, where $x$ is an element

The rapid advancement of video editing technology has enabled the development of
highly realistic and persuasive videos. These convincing videos have far-reaching
implications for artificial intelligence systems, human perception, and overall
society. Although this technology has the potential to bring numerous benefits,
it also poses a significant threat to society if exploited maliciously. In this study,
we provide a comprehensive overview of the key challenges and obstacles in creating
convincing videos, followed by a detailed examination of the current state of
research in the field, including the methods employed to evaluate and verify the
realism of video content. We also discuss the associated challenges and potential
applications of this technology and propose future directions for further
research and development in this area.

This study explores the application of minimal length Heisenberg algebra and squeezed coherent states of movement in the analysis of ions confined within a quadrupole ion trap. The investigation demonstrates that the lower limit of the minimal length scale can be determined through the adjustment of the electric field within the ion trap to meet specific requirements. By assuming that the ions are non-relativistic and utilizing the Tietz particle model in the minimal length Heisenberg algebra, the motion of the ions in the ion trap is studied. The results reveal that the minimal length introduces an asymmetry in the motion of the ions, which can be characterized by the mean square position and momentum of the ions. The analysis also shows that the minimal length impacts the frequency of the ion's oscillation and the precision of the position of the ion. Furthermore, the squeezed coherent states of movement of the ions in the ion trap are examined. The study provides a detailed analysis of the quadrature variances of the ion's movement in the ion trap within the framework of the minimal length Heisenberg algebra, which can be used to understand the squeezing behavior of the ion's movement in the ion trap.

Neuroscience simulations are becoming increasingly complex, driving the need for efficient high-performance computing resources. To achieve this, researchers must optimize the selection of computer architecture, algorithm, and hardware settings, often a daunting task. Fortunately, the "Learning to Learn" paradigm can automate this process, efficiently exploring the optimal hyper-parameter configuration for specific computing systems. We have successfully applied this paradigm to optimize the domain-specific domain-wall model for a specific type of high-performance computing system, the Summit supercomputer. Our findings indicate that optimized settings can significantly reduce the computational time required for domain-wall simulations, with estimated savings of 3 to 4 orders of magnitude.

Camouflaged object segmentation in complex real-world environments is a difficult task, often necessitating a deep understanding of objects and their surroundings. This insights-based approach can lead to biased segmentation results. To address this issue, a new dataset has been created, featuring images of camouflaged objects in unaltered, unedited environments, with no prior knowledge or assumptions. This dataset, CAMO, consists of 1,668 high-quality images, with both object masks and background information provided. A novel segmentation approach, based on saliency prediction, has been designed to tackle the camouflaged object segmentation challenge, with promising results demonstrated on the CAMO dataset. To further advance this field, a comprehensive segmentation benchmark has been established, incorporating camouflaged object datasets from multiple categories.

The Lorentz symmetry breakdown, characterized by significant violations, has far-reaching implications for multiple physical phenomena. Specifically, the effects of Lorentz infringement on superconductivity are significant and warrant exploration. This study delves into the superconductivity phase transition under the influence of Lorentz symmetry breakdown. Employing a modified free energy function that incorporates Lorentz symmetry breakdown parameters, the modified free energy equation is derived. Subsequently, the maximum current density, the critical current density, and the corresponding critical temperature are calculated. These results indicate that both the maximum and critical current densities and critical temperature increase with increasing $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$, with the effect of $\theta_1$ being more pronounced.

To improve the reliability of machine learning models, we need to identify and address "defects" - decisions that are incorrect but legitimate in certain contexts. Current methods for detecting these issues, such as using human annotator pairs, are resource-intensive and often overlook the broader impact of these errors. To address this, we've developed a new method for detecting defects that involves having a large group of people identify incorrect outputs from AI models and then providing detailed explanations for each incorrect response. Our approach allows us to identify a substantial number of previously undetected defects and validate the accuracy of these "crowd reports" by comparing them with independent verification from co-annotator pairs.

Deep learning object classification systems are often vulnerable to adversarial attacks due to overfitting. To counter this, we developed a stochastic choice routing method that allows multiple class outputs with low confidence to select from a broader set of possibilities, thereby reducing overfitting and improving robustness. This approach involves a dynamic routing module that aggregates high-level semantic features from multiple instance-level predictions. By introducing learnable weights, the module directs multiple instance features toward a specific class, effectively balancing the confidence level of each feature. The proposed routing mechanism can be seamlessly integrated into existing deep neural networks and has been successfully applied to ResNet and ResNet50, yielding improved performance on standard benchmarks and robustness tests.

The FGSM adversarial preparation method is widely used in crafting adversarial examples, however, it often results in overly complex features in the intermediate layers, which subsequently causes significant overfitting issues. To address this problem, we propose a novel FGSM preparation method, known as ZeroGrad, that incorporates L2-norm regularization in the gradient domain to effectively suppress small gradients. This method effectively eliminates high-frequency noise and its effectiveness is comparable to existing approaches, such as Dropout and weight decay. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that ZeroGrad has a positive impact on the robustness of FGSM-generated adversarial examples against white-box and black-box attacks.

Our analysis reveals that the Thakurta metric, which was initially used to describe black holes formed from collapsing star cores, does not apply to black holes originating from the early universe.  Consequently, the restrictions imposed by the LIGO-Virgo observations hold little bearing on the notion of primordial black holes (PBHs) having a mass close to the solar mass.  The findings of the current study diverge from those presented in the Thakurta 1972 paper, which initially described the referenced metric.  The discrepancy stems from the fact that the universe's background spacetime, as opposed to the star core, supports a flat space; consequently, the appropriate metric is the Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker metric, which was overlooked in the 1972 paper.

Optimization techniques have been developed to overcome the challenges of noisy evaluation functions, such as those in machine learning and evolutionary computation. However, the changing nature of optimal solutions in these problems, known as persistent asset dynamics, can significantly impact the effectiveness of these methods. In this study, we investigate how different noise categories, including drift, shift, and high-frequency noise, affect the performance of three hybrid optimization algorithms: a genetic algorithm paired with Newton's method, a genetic algorithm paired with the quasi-Newton BFGS algorithm, and the CMA-ES algorithm. Our findings are based on a detailed analysis of the expected convergence time of each method, and we identify the optimal parameters for each algorithm under various noise conditions.

A key objective in homomorphic encryption is achieving full encryption homomorphism. However, given the significant computational burden associated with current completely homomorphic encryption schemes (such as those by Gentry, Halevi, and Reynolds, and Marathe et al.), it is typically applied only to simple circuits. In an effort to address this limitation, we developed a new scheme based on the Ring-LWE problem, which can efficiently encrypt complex programs, including those written in Turing machine code, provided the programs are structured in a tree-like format. Our proposed scheme is designed to be bootstrappable and supports both deterministic and probabilistic polynomial-time computations. It is also equipped with a mechanism for secure evaluation key expansion, allowing it to handle computations with varying input sizes without additional parameter settings.

A collection of solvable random matrix problems is developed within the framework of deformed harmonic oscillators, where an external non-linear potential influences the eigenvalue distributions. The associated Schrödinger operators form a solvable hierarchy, allowing for the derivation of their eigenvalues through a systematic, parameter-dependent method based on analytic continuation. We focus on the statistical properties of the corresponding random matrix ensembles and examine how the external potential affects their eigenvalue distributions. The potential considered is a logarithmic function, which is a common characteristic of Gaussian ensembles and has been observed in physical systems as a natural, fundamental aspect.

Quantum relationships are a crucial component in designing quantum technologies, and their characterization is vital for understanding quantum circuits. We investigate and quantify quantum connections through entanglement and monogamy in a two-qutrit spin system. Our findings reveal that the entanglement monogamy bound is met, and it provides a comprehensive framework for understanding three-mode correlations by breaking them down into within-and-between subspace components. Utilizing a controlled classical field approach, we experimentally demonstrate that the system's quantum connections can be manipulated and control strategies are developed to optimize these connections.

In 1964, Bell demonstrated that hidden variable theories cannot surpass the predictions made by quantum mechanics in correlations.  Despite this, many attempts have been made to develop new hidden variable theories capable of surpassing quantum limits.  A new study proposes a different approach: to develop a theory of quantum mechanics that is locally composite, meaning it can be broken down into separate components operating over distinct spatial locations.  A key feature of this theory is that it predicts a non-ideal EPR singlet-state correlation, where two particles' properties are not perfectly correlated.  This work explores the implications of such a theory and the potential for experimental verification.  A novel state, referred to as the "Huang state," serves as a testbed for detecting non-ideal EPR correlations.  A state that is close to the ideal correlation, but still exhibits some degree of imperfection, the Huang state is characterized by a high level of entanglement between two particles.  This work provides a method for using the Huang state to detect non-ideal EPR correlations and the implications for such a theory.

We introduce StyleGAN-V, a generative model capable of creating an infinite variety of high-quality videos with diverse styles and lengths. This comprehensive model is designed to work with a single input image and can be trained without any pre-existing video data. We propose a novel video generation framework that utilizes a single image and can produce an unlimited variety of high-quality videos with diverse styles and lengths. To achieve this, we employ a combination of techniques, including a novel rendering layer, a new clip-based latent space, and a range of innovative training strategies. We demonstrate that our approach enables StyleGAN-V to generate high-quality videos with moving objects and seamless transitions. We show that our model can produce a wide range of video features, such as camera angles, lighting, and special effects, and can be easily adaptable to various applications. We compare our results with existing video generation models and show that our approach delivers superior performance, achieving state-of-the-art results with lower memory usage. We also highlight the potential of StyleGAN-V to address a range of practical challenges in video editing and production.

Let $q$ be an odd prime power, with $Q = q^2$, and let $\eta(q)$ be the Dirichlet character defined by the map $x \mapsto (-1)^{(x^3 + 1) / 2}$. The authors establish the degree of the $\eta(q)$-Sato-Tate group as $\frac{3}{\pi} \eta(q) \log q + O(1)$. This result leads to a novel bound on the $\eta(q)$-Sato-Tate density, which is $\frac{3}{\pi} \eta(q) + O(1)$. The authors further prove that the degree of the $\eta(q)$-Sato-Tate measure is $\frac{3}{\pi} \eta(q) + O(1)$. The results are derived by combining the $\eta(q)$-Sato-Tate factors with the $\psi(q)$-Sato-Tate factors, utilizing the method of moments.

Accurate dose estimation is crucial for cancer treatment and requires precise methods for measuring ionizing radiation exposure.  Traditionally used for thousands of years, dosimetry has largely remained manual, with the use of thin window glass phantoms and thermoluminescent dosimetry (TLD) being the standard.  While digital dosimetry offers improved accuracy, it still relies heavily on human interaction.  Recent advancements in deep learning have enabled the development of automated methods for dose estimation, with this work presenting a novel approach that leverages deep learning to estimate the date of radiation exposure with high accuracy and precision.  Our model was trained on a dataset of images of TLD-chips, with the goal of predicting the date of radiation exposure, with the results showing a high degree of accuracy and precision in predicting the date of radiation exposure, with the model performing well on unseen data and showing high transferability across different image resolutions.

Let $M$ be an $n$-dimensional compact smooth Riemannian manifold, and consider the problem of finding a non-negative function $u$ that minimizes the functional among all non-negative functions in the Sobolev-Orlicz space, where the Sobolev norm is defined using the Bessel potential operator. The functional's exponents $\alpha$ and $\beta$ may fluctuate, leading to a singular problem. Assuming $p_1, p_{\infty} < \infty$, we prove the existence of a non-negative solution $u$ under the condition that $p_{\infty}<\alpha<\frac{n}{n-1}$, $p_1<\frac{n}{\alpha}$, and $p_{\infty},\alpha\in(1,\infty)$.

A computer algorithm was developed to generate digital images that mimic X-ray patterns produced by cone beam CT scanners using kilovolt (kV) X-rays. The simulator, named Fastcat Sim, was based on the Fastcat phantom and was designed to accurately model the device's X-ray cone angles and beam kinetics. The performance of another simulator, Fastcat Sim, in comparison to actual data from a real cone beam CT scanner using MV photons was evaluated. The results showed that Fastcat Sim effectively simulated MV beam cone angles and photon energy spectra. However, the accuracy of MV photon energy spectra was relatively low, especially when the energy level was far from the center of the beam.

In recent years, Explainable Reinforcement Learning (XRL) has emerged as a growing field due to the increasing demand for transparency in decision-making. Reinforcement learning models, which are increasingly employed in critical applications, require explainability to ensure that their decision-making processes are transparent. LIME, a widely used technique for individual instance explanation, has been applied to various machine learning tasks. However, its application in time-series reinforcement learning environments is complicated by the dynamic nature of these environments, making it difficult to generate accurate explanations. This research proposes a novel stability-based approach to LIME, which is tailored to time-series reinforcement learning environments and addresses the challenges posed by their dynamic nature. The proposed technique, S-LIME, calculates explanations based on the most stable sequences of actions and states, rather than a fixed point. By doing so, S-LIME mitigates the inaccuracies that arise from the application of traditional LIME in time-series reinforcement learning environments. The results of our experiments, which were conducted in a simulated environment, demonstrate the effectiveness of S-LIME and pave the way for its application in real-world time-series reinforcement learning environments.

To improve human accuracy in categorizing visual images, we developed a technique that not only trains people to recognize categories but also teaches them why they are making incorrect distinctions. By using this method, we found that participants who received informative feedback became more confident in their ability to classify complex objects and achieved better results than those who only received general training. This technique can be used to enhance various types of categorization skills.

TbInO$_3$ is a rare-earth spiral spin-liquid candidate with a Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction. Using advanced computational methods, we investigated the crystal and vibronic properties of TbInO$_3$. We discovered that its crystal-field excitations are influenced by the specific arrangement of rare-earth ions in the crystal structure. Notably, two specific crystal-field modes exhibit distinct patterns due to the non-standard arrangement of Tb$^{3+}$ ions. Furthermore, we found that specific vibrational modes contribute to the rare-earth electronic structure through the coupling of vibronic and Raman scattering processes. These findings provide a foundation for further research into the crystal-field and spin-liquid properties of TbInO$_3$.

We apply a novel, two-part convexity principle to address the evolution of compact hypersurfaces moving at a rate equal to the power of their mean curvature. By focusing on the power-of-mean curvature equation, we expand upon earlier research concerning curvature flows and their ability to preserve convex shapes. Specifically, we examine the situation where the rate of the flow is proportional to either the minimum or the maximum of its mean curvature, and demonstrate that convex hypersurfaces undergo flat, or "mean convex/minimally convex," collapse respectively.

A new approach to image convolution has been proposed, which transforms the process into the frequency domain to improve efficiency, but this is achieved without the need for the traditional Fourier transform. Instead, a unique factorization called the IQFT is utilized. Notably, this method does not require the Fourier coefficients to be computed beforehand. By contrast, a novel deep neural network architecture is introduced, which performs convolution, normalization, and non-linearity directly in the spectrum domain, thereby streamlining the traditional convolutional neural network workflow. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this spectral-based approach, yielding faster inference times and comparable performance to traditional convolutional neural networks.

The objective of the image grouping task is to categorize pixels into groups based on similar texture, color, and shape characteristics. This information is crucial for downstream applications, such as texture analysis and image segmentation. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have significantly impacted computer vision, and the extension of deep neural networks to image grouping has been a logical next step. Nevertheless, existing deep image grouping methods are plagued by high computational requirements and the absence of multi-layer optimization. To address this, we introduce a novel framework, DeepCluE, which integrates a unique set of convolutional operators and a novel grouping loss function optimized across multiple layers. This approach enables the efficient propagation of information between layers, leading to the discovery of more refined grouping patterns. Furthermore, our proposed DeepCluE framework demonstrates superior performance on various image grouping tasks, outperforming state-of-the-art methods across multiple datasets.

The concept of social risk refers to the likelihood of unpredictable events triggering widespread unrest in a society. By analyzing social media and news outlets in real-time, it is possible to identify the underlying factors contributing to this risk. This research presents a comprehensive framework for monitoring and analyzing a society's risk level in a structured and continuous manner. Key elements of this framework include (1) a system for gathering data from multiple news sources using social media platforms, (2) an algorithm for automatically categorizing news content, (3) a model for analyzing knowledge networks to track connections between various events, and (4) a system for generating an interactive visual interface that displays an evolving society's risk map. This framework was successfully tested on a large-scale dataset of 1.7 million articles from 37 news sources in Indonesia, and the results were presented to the public and to the Indonesian government in an easily accessible format.

Data-driven applications rely heavily on categorization. With the advent of abundant and complex data, it's become increasingly difficult for humans to effectively categorize objects. As a result, automated categorization methods have gained prominence. The proposed categorization method leverages the strengths of unsupervised machine learning and computational topology to analyze objects. Specifically, the method employs persistent homology to analyze the features of various objects. The proposed method's effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to a real-world dataset, specifically an image dataset consisting of 1,210 images of 120 unique categories, sourced from the Stanford ImageNet Legacy Dataset.
We show that the contrasimilarity relation can be represented as a strategic game and prove the player has at least two optimal strategies.

The aim of this paper is to create a visual representation that illustrates the concept of string 2-groups. Notably, selecting the visual representation over the choice of which object in the 2-group corresponds to the identity element results in a more inclusive and broader category of string groups. Consequently, this approach leads to a more comprehensive category of groupoids that can be used to describe string field theory through its classical solutions. As an initial step towards exploring this idea, we examine the string 2-group associated with the De Sitter IIB groupoid. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of this string 2-group for the associated string field theory.

Using double pair plasma consisting of cold positrons and negative ions, the nonlinear propagation of ion-acoustic waves has been analyzed. Positrons behave as heavy, warm particles, while electrons are assumed to be cold. By employing the reductive perturbation method, the nonlinear Schr\"{o}ndinger equation is derived. It is found that the inclusion of warm positrons can generate rogue waves through the formation of modulational instability, and the presence of warm electrons can also produce soliton-rogue waves. Furthermore, the ion-acoustic rogue waves are greatly affected by variations in plasma density, temperature, and the non-extensive parameter for the warm electrons, and the ion-acoustic rogue waves are observed to be more intense in the context of a double pair plasma.

A novel approach to model the Alfvén wave parametric decay instability in a plasma is proposed by integrating kinetic theory with fluid models. Specifically, the magnetic field components are captured using a fluid model, whereas the kinetic description is restricted to a single species. To account for the Alfvén wave's varying amplitude, the model employs an initial condition derived from linear analysis and a simulation technique to track the maximum wave amplitude. Following the decay into a higher frequency Alfvén wave and ion Bernstein modes due to the initial condition's transient phase, a stable equilibrium is achieved through energy transfer from the primary wave to the excited modes.

We have investigated the gravitational instability of a weakly magnetized, thread-like nebula composed of molecular gas and dust, and how it affects ambipolar diffusion. This type of nebula can be found in the center of molecular filaments and is a common feature in star-forming regions. Our analysis focuses on a cold, weakly magnetized, and rotating filament with a non-uniform distribution of gas and dust, and includes ambipolar diffusion. We derived the time-dependent nonlinear equations governing the gas and dust density, and the magnetic field, and used them to calculate the growth rate of instability. Our findings show that ambipolar diffusion significantly increases the growth rate of gravitational instability, and that this effect is most pronounced in longer filaments. We also found that the inclusion of ambipolar diffusion reduces the critical magnetic field required for instability, and that this critical field is a key factor in determining the outcome of gravitational instability. Our analysis suggests that ambipolar diffusion can lead to the formation of star clusters in the center of molecular filaments.

The Zeno and anti-Zeno effects occur when repeated measurements significantly speed up or delay a quantum system's evolution, respectively. This study explores these effects within the dynamic Decoherence-Induced Superselection (DIS) model. By focusing on the strong coupling regime, it examines how repeated measurements influence the transition probability of an excited state in a two-state system. Our findings reveal that anti-Zeno effects prevail in this regime, contradicting previous studies. To further validate these results, a theoretical analysis is combined with a numerical simulation. This work expands the theoretical understanding of the Zeno and anti-Zeno effects to include the strong coupling regime.

This research investigates the behavior of a Heisenberg spin chain with Dzyaloshinsky-Moriya interactions and an applied magnetic field that varies along the chain. Key findings are derived from a combination of analytical and numerical techniques, such as series expansion and matrix product state methods. Specifically, the study focuses on a model with PBC, examining how the system's properties change as the magnetic field strength increases. Notably, the research reveals a set of critical points at which the ground state undergoes significant changes, including phase transitions that may be either discontinuous or continuous. A detailed analysis of these transitions is provided, including their effects on various physical properties. Additionally, the study explores a related problem involving a system with open boundaries, where researchers aim to determine the thermal properties of the system. A key finding is that the system's energy and specific heat exhibit distinct peaks at specific temperatures, depending on the magnetic field strength. A detailed analysis is presented to support these results.

This study presents a groundbreaking approach for multi-robot path planning in distributed scenarios, with a focus on safety and viability. This method addresses the limitations of traditional approaches such as the Motion Planning Toolkit, which are plagued by undeterminability issues in multi-robot settings. To overcome this, our research introduces a novel framework based on Linear Safe Passage, a concept that ensures the safety of multiple robots by defining a safe region. To enhance the scalability of the algorithm, its application is divided among a network of computing agents, each responsible for a subset of the mission objectives. To achieve this distributed goal, our team designed a novel Viability Guarantee algorithm, which employs the Linear Safe Passage concept to ensure the completion of missions in a timely and safe manner. This algorithm was successfully implemented in a multi-robot scenario involving a swarm of quadrotors, with each robot navigating to a target location while avoiding collisions with other robots. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the Viability Guarantee algorithm, with each robot successfully completing its mission, highlighting the potential of the Linear Safe Passage concept for multi-robot path planning in distributed systems.

Unsupervised domain transfer is a crucial task in making simulation models applicable to real-world environments without needing human supervision. The path detection task within this area focuses on identifying the optimal route within a scene. Existing solutions primarily utilize straightforward, highly structured simulations like game environments. However, real-world settings are significantly more complex and require immediate path detection. This paper presents CARLANE, a comprehensive benchmark that enables domain transfer for path detection across various real-world domains. The developed methods effectively close the gap between simulated and real-world environments by leveraging adversarial learning to account for differences in appearance and scene structure. Evaluations on CARLANE showcase substantial performance enhancements over existing solutions, demonstrating up to a 25% boost in ADE-F score and 75% reduction in end-to-end inference time.

Our research involves studying how particles affect contact angle on hydrogels. Theoretical models are developed to explain the impact of particle size and concentration on the apparent contact angle. Experimental data from hydrogels containing silica particles are compared to the adjusted contact angle, showing good match in both cases. One of the key findings is that for small particles relative to the gel pore size, the apparent contact angle diminishes at a rate slower than square of the particle volume fraction. This effect enables us to control the contact angle through particle addition without compromising water absorption capacity of hydrogels.

The abrupt shift to online learning brought on by the COVID pandemic exposed students to unprecedented challenges, leading to a significant decline in learning effectiveness and overall well-being.  Consequently, understanding how students' behavior and performance changed during this period has become a pressing concern.  To address this issue, this study analyzed data from a comprehensive online platform used by over 2.5 million students worldwide, examining how students' behavior and performance evolved over the course of the pandemic.  Our findings reveal that while academic achievement remained relatively stable, engagement significantly declined in response to the pandemic, with the decline accelerating over time.  Furthermore, we discovered that students' behavior and performance are closely intertwined, with certain patterns of engagement predicting future academic outcomes.  Our analysis also revealed that students' motivation to learn is a persistent motivator, as they tend to engage in activities driven by a desire to succeed.  These insights not only provide a deeper understanding of students' behavior during the pandemic, but also offer practical guidance for educators seeking to enhance teaching effectiveness and improve learning outcomes.

The wind speed measurement system on the Swift observatory's rotating wheel uses an antenna's Doppler effect to detect changes in speed, allowing the measurement of the wheel's rotation rate and thereby avoiding potential collisions with debris in orbit. This system, which has been in operation since 2009, was initially based on a simple measurement technique. However, a more advanced method utilizing autoregressive modeling was developed to improve the measurement, significantly reducing inconsistencies and inaccuracies in measurement. This new algorithm utilizes data from the L-band radar and the horizontal channel of the quick-look plot, which shows a strong correlation between measured and actual wind speeds.

We have analyzed the properties of UBC 274, a cluster in the fourth quadrant, utilizing data from Gaia EDR3, V-band images, and the ALMA telescope. Our findings reveal that UBC 274 is a cluster in the process of disruption, comprising a stellar component and a diffuse gas cloud. The star distribution indicates a mass within the range of 1000 to 2000 solar masses, with a half-mass relaxation time of approximately 0.03 million years. The gas cloud has a total mass of approximately 15 solar masses, with a gas surface density of about 0.05 solar masses per square parsec, and a gas velocity dispersion of roughly 0.2 kilometers per second. The radial distribution of the gas is consistent with the presence of a two-component gas disk, with a more massive inner component and a smaller outer component. The elemental composition of the gas, as determined by ALMA, reveals a metallicity of about 0.6 times the solar value, with a total hydrogen abundance of about 0.7. The gas in UBC 274 is likely the result of the disruption of its original cluster, with the gas forming as a result of the destruction of its original stars. The origin of the gas is also likely the result of the destruction of its original molecular clouds, with the gas then being reformed into a molecular cloud. The primary metric for assessing the quality of parallel corpora is bilingual evaluation web tool (BlewT), which employs artificial translations to gauge human performance in creating high-quality translations. This study reexamines the functionality of BlewT and reveals that its evaluations heavily favor systems producing accurate word orders. Consequently, a system utilizing effective ordering techniques can achieve high scores without achieving satisfactory translations. To address this issue and improve bitext assessment, we introduce two novel metrics: (i) the structure-based evaluation metric, which evaluates bitexts on a higher level of linguistic structure, and (ii) the translation memory-based metric, which assesses bitexts on a smaller scale of vocabulary units. These proposed metrics are intended to evaluate bitexts based on their overall meaning rather than individual word arrangement.

Recent research has shown that the entanglement of quantum spin chains can be manipulated by controlling the strength of specific interactions. This study explores a variation of a well-known model where a spin chain is influenced by both neighboring interactions and a controlled, dissipation-based mechanism. This dissipation effect is triggered by the spin values at specific points on the chain. By studying the resulting many-body quantum state, researchers found that the entanglement levels can be adjusted through the dissipation strength. This effect is caused by the way dissipation interacts with other spin interactions, influencing the state's evolution. As a result, the impact of dissipation on entanglement can be controlled, leading to a gradual shift from increased levels to decreased levels. This study also found that the state's behavior can be explained by the gradual shift from increased levels to decreased levels within specific regions of the spin chain.

The interaction between electrons and their spin-orbit properties is a crucial factor determining the behavior of electrons within the flat bands found in transition metal dichalcogenide heterostructures. Researchers have conducted a comprehensive analysis of the effects of this interaction using a tight-binding model, which reveals that it significantly influences the electronic properties of these systems. The findings indicate that the resulting electron spin polarization is highly sensitive to the specific dimensions and composition of the structure, thereby presenting a promising approach for its manipulation.

A new quantum filter is proposed, capable of filtering quantum bits in reservoir computing systems consisting of a single oscillation. The proposed filter utilizes a combination of quantum gates and environmental interactions, specifically the amplitude damping process, on a single qubit. The performance of the filter is evaluated by assessing the recovery of entangled states in noisy environments, utilizing numerical and analytical methods. The results show that the filter can successfully restore entangled states with high accuracy across a wide range of noise settings, as measured by the fidelity of the filtered states. The filter's ability to restore entangled states depends on the reservoir's size and the time step used in the filtering process, and is also sensitive to the noise settings. The proposed filter has potential applications in enhancing the performance of quantum neural networks.

High-quality epitaxial GaN-on-silicon wafers offer a promising option for
creating highly integrated and efficient single-photon devices. The existing
production limitations of these high-quality materials stem from the challenging
crystal growth process on insulating substrates. To address this issue, our
study proposes a novel method for enhancing the performance of these high-quality
single-photon devices by optimizing the sapphire substrate with a high-temperature
diffused ion implantation process. By accurately controlling the implanting
conditions, it is possible to selectively create a pathway for efficient light
coupling between the GaN and the silicon substrate without compromising the light
emitting properties. The results show that a reliable method for confining atoms on
GaN-on-sapphire substrates has been developed, which can withstand high temperatures
(600°C) and laser intensities, while maintaining a strong optical response. The strong
reduction in optical response observed at high temperatures is significantly reduced
by an order of magnitude, from 80% to 5%, when an ion-implanted region is used. The
study also demonstrates that a pathway for light coupling between the GaN and the
underlying substrate can be created, which can be achieved by carefully controlling
the implanting conditions.

This research introduces a numerical study on the use of Lagrange and mixed finite elements for solving an elliptic PDE. The Lagrange approach employs unstructured grids and two types of polynomial order, while the mixed formulation incorporates the DG-M0 method with divergence and curl constraints. The study aims to compare the convergence rates of these finite element schemes by analyzing $L^2$ and $H(D^2)$ norms for both the primary and flux variables. The numerical results demonstrate comparable performance between the two methods, with the addition of mixed elements benefiting from improved $L^2$ norm convergence for flux variables. The study further includes simulations of Stokes flow and Maxwell equations, with the MFEM library used for all numerical implementations.

We investigate the cosmological evolution of a specific dark energy model featuring sign-alterable interactions, and a novel scenario is explored in detail. The model's evolution equations are resolved analytically for the sign-alterable model, and the resulting solutions are analyzed for their physical implications. Additionally, we employ two distinct methods to derive the equation of state parameter ω in both scenarios, and use the statefinder diagnostics to characterize the model's evolution. The results indicate that the model's behavior differs qualitatively from that of the cosmological constant model, and we discuss the implications of these findings for our understanding of the universe's evolution.

The collision of a star with a supermassive black hole creates a shock that can accelerate particles, producing a brief burst of electromagnetic radiation. We have developed a model to estimate the electromagnetic output of these bursts, specifically focusing on the non-thermal radio flares that appear in the X-ray afterglow of TDEs. By applying this model to the TDE of NGC 4594's star, we found that the shock's non-thermal electrons are ejected perpendicular to the shock's direction, resulting in a brief, intense burst of electromagnetic radiation. This model's predictions are consistent with the electromagnetic output of these shocks, specifically the synchrotron radiation, and suggest that the low-frequency radio bursts are likely caused by the shock's particle acceleration. This model's predictions are also consistent with the recently observed radio bursts from the TDE of NGC 5905's star, suggesting that the low-frequency radio emission is caused by the shock's particle acceleration. This finding implies that the shock's particle acceleration is widespread in these types of shock systems.

The purpose of this paper is to introduce a novel approach for modeling acoustic bubble interactions in nonlinear flow. We have developed a time-domain numerical method for simulating the effects of micro-bubbles on acoustic waves. Our model is based on the Rayleigh-Inners equation, which describes the acoustic response of a micro-bubble in terms of a nonlinear acoustic wave. We have applied this model to various acoustic frequencies, ranging from 5 kHz to 20 kHz, and observed how its acoustic response changes in different regimes. We have also investigated the effects of micro-bubble size, including the effects of size distribution and the effects of multiple bubbles. Our findings suggest that the micro-bubbles' resonance frequency is highly sensitive to their size, and that the acoustic response is heavily influenced by the size distribution of the micro-bubbles.

In our research, we introduce a cutting-edge, multimodal model for tension
recognition, combining the latest advances in multimodal AI and attention
techniques. Our model is trained on a comprehensive dataset of human thermal
and audio data, collected during a series of stress tests. The results of our
experiments demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, outperforming previous
models in the same domain. Furthermore, we present a novel method for using
emotion acknowledgment as a supplementary task to enhance the accuracy of
tension identification, which achieves the highest performance to date.

Developing intelligent systems to operate in real-world environments effectively is a significant challenge. The PanGEA framework is an innovative tool that utilizes artificial data augmentation to enhance the capabilities of graph neural networks in processing large, dynamic, and unstructured real-world environments. This approach is based on the idea that real-world environments are similar to virtual ones in terms of their complexity, requiring a more realistic and efficient training environment for machine learning algorithms. The PanGEA framework is a user-friendly annotation toolkit that enables users to create artificial data for machine learning models using a virtual environment. The framework's modular design and customization options make it highly flexible, allowing users to modify and expand it according to their needs.

We have developed a model to study the evolution of elliptical galaxies by taking into account the variation of the stellar initial mass function (IMF) with metallicity and its impact on star formation timescales. We have found that the variation of the IMF with metallicity is a key factor in star formation timescales, particularly for more metal-poor environments. Our model shows that the timescales required to form a galaxy with the same final mass are longer in metal-poor environments compared to metal-rich environments. We have used our model to investigate the potential for multiple generations of stars within elliptical galaxies and observed that, for a given galaxy mass, the number of generations of stars increases with the metallicity of the host galaxy. We have discovered that, for more metal-rich environments, the number of generations of stars is significantly reduced, whereas the number of generations of stars is only slightly affected by the host galaxy's metallicity in less metal-rich environments. We have also found that, for more metal-rich environments, the number of type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) is significantly reduced, whereas the number of SNe Ia is only slightly affected by the host galaxy's metallicity in less metal-rich environments.

Recent advances in compressive sensing technology have led to the development of innovative image reconstruction algorithms, enabling accurate image recovery from lower sensor sampling rates. Current solutions, however, are limited in their ability to generalize to various images, and often fall short in handling complex scenarios involving multiple objects and backgrounds. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel image representation framework that leverages the collective representation of images through sparse coding in a self-expressive model. This approach also incorporates non-linear image constraints and is optimized using an iterative dual update framework. The proposed method has been extensively evaluated on both synthetic and real-world images, demonstrating superior image reconstruction quality compared to existing solutions.

The human face is comprised of numerous distinct regions, each bearing unique characteristics of facial skin problems. Current facial skin analysis methods typically segment and identify individual types of skin issues, but fail to effectively capture the distinct patterns of each area. To address this limitation, we introduce RethNet, a novel network architecture inspired by medical diagnosis, which learns to identify skin problems on a per-area basis by analyzing the distinct features of each region. Leveraging the insights from both the original skin map and the learned region-specific patterns, RethNet generates a comprehensive skin analysis. To improve the model's adaptability to new skin regions, we propose a transfer learning approach that enables RethNet to effectively recognize unknown skin issues. Comprehensive experiments on multiple public datasets demonstrate that RethNet outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both known and unknown skin issue recognition tasks.

Our research delves into the efficiency of sequential decoding for polarized accumulation codes (PAC codes), a class that includes DA codes. Although DA codes have been extensively studied, PAC codes were only recently introduced due to computational limitations in analyzing their structural properties. We have developed efficient methods to calculate the structural properties of PAC codes, including their distance distribution and weight hierarchy. Using these findings, we can now generate and verify the validity of PAC code designs. We have also developed a new search algorithm to find optimal PAC code designs that maximize the minimum distance, achieving a success rate of 100% for certain block lengths and error rates. In terms of complexity, we have found that the number of possible weight assignments for PAC codes grows polynomially with the block length. Building on this finding, we have developed a new decoding algorithm for PAC codes that significantly outperforms the standard sequential decoding approach.

Online learning platforms face difficulties due to "cold-start" users, who experience barriers to entry. To address this issue, a new approach called sequential suggestions is proposed, which aims to retain users by offering recommended learning steps. However, this strategy is complex and requires significant resources. To improve efficiency, a Meta Transitional Education (MTE) framework is developed, which transitions users through suggested content while keeping costs in check. The framework's effectiveness is evaluated using a cost function that considers user retention and system expenditure, and its behavior is analyzed under different constraints. Results from the experimental data show that the proposed framework successfully balances user retention and system profitability.

Galactic cosmic rays with energies exceeding 100 TeV, referred to as ultra high energy galactic rays (UHEGRs), are a relatively understudied aspect of high-energy astrophysics. Despite numerous theories on their origin, no single model has gained widespread acceptance. The uncertainty surrounding their existence, however, stems from the UHEGR spectrum's concordance with the extragalactic ultrahigh energy cosmic ray horizon cross-section. This paper presents a simple extension to the standard UHEGR model, incorporating two key elements: the consideration of UHEGRs' absorption in molecular clouds and the inclusion of UHEGRs' escape from the galaxy.

The Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) mission, to be launched in 2021, aims to collide a small spacecraft with a planet-crossing asteroid to change its trajectory and prevent a potential collision with Earth. Researchers have analyzed the effect of the impactor's shape on the ejected material and momentum transfer, using both analytical and numerical methods. The results indicate that the projectile's shape affects the ejection angle of the material, with significant implications for the overall momentum transfer, particularly in cases where the impactor's center of mass does not align with its geometric center. The findings, obtained through simulations and calculations, show that the off-center momentum is substantial and, in some cases, can reach up to 20% of the impact's overall momentum. This discovery has important implications for the DART mission, as it may affect the overall momentum transfer, but further simulations are required to provide a more accurate estimate.

In autonomous driving, through-the-windshield (TWS) recognition is a critical challenge that involves identifying operators in various states. To address this, researchers have developed the Mertens Unfolded Network (MU-Net), a data-driven approach that enables TWS recognition. MU-Net is designed to capture and analyze dynamic interval data from multiple sources, including static and dynamic characteristics. The network consists of three key components: an unfolded network that extracts and aggregates features, a recognition module that generates classification labels, and an association module that determines the number of individuals detected from multiple TWS cameras. In a comparative study, MU-Net demonstrated superior performance compared to existing methods, with a significant improvement of 4.8% in F1-score.

This study delves into the underutilized aspect of text descriptions in software repositories. Focusing on 24 prominent programming languages, including their core features and extensive range of libraries, we conducted an extensive content analysis of 592,000+ text entries. Our analysis revealed notable differences in writing styles, including distinct variations within each language community. Notably, our research uncovered distinct textorial patterns, including humor, sarcasm, and the use of emojis. Utilizing advanced network analysis techniques, we mapped the complex interplay between language communities. Our findings suggest that text descriptions can serve as a valuable resource for identifying key language trends, predicting community growth, and facilitating cross-language collaboration. Our findings indicate that certain languages prioritize technical details, while others focus on utility and community engagement. Our research has the potential to inform developers about relevant communities, ultimately guiding informed language choices. Ultimately, our analysis highlights the potential of text-based information in software repositories, recommending further research in this area.

Causal inference in situations with missing essential covariates and incomplete outcomes is a complex issue. To address this, we developed a novel approach of hierarchical estimators that combine data with and without the essential information, using an example from a randomized trial as inspiration. By applying this framework, we identified a missing essential moderator in a study and discovered that a treatment's effect remained unchanged. This breakthrough was achieved in spite of significant missing essential data (50%) and incomplete outcomes (20%).

The accuracy of certain approximations for the first kind under the condition that $|\sinh(x)|<1$ has been examined. These approximations involve using the inverse hyperbolic tangent function, specifically in the forms $\sum_{j=1}^p a_j \text{inhartan}(x/j^2)$ and $\sum_{j=1}^p b_j \text{inhartan}(x/j^2)$, where $a_j$, $b_j$ are real constants and $x$ is a real number. Research has shown that these approximations are not always accurate, specifically for large values of $p$, regardless of the choice of $a_j$ and $b_j$. In fact, the method used to create these approximations does not produce convergent results, and the method used to create a different approximation is not applicable in all cases. In an effort to create a convergent series, the terms were adjusted by multiplying them by the terms' derivatives. However, the method used to create a different approximation is not applicable in all cases. Certain series were found to be convergent, including a series with coefficients that are related to the third and fifth Bernoulli numbers, and the series with $p=4$ and $a_j$ as the sequence of the third and fifth Bernoulli numbers' square values divided by $j^2$ is also convergent.

Deep learning models are typically trained using a combination of supervised and unsupervised techniques.  While supervised methods like supervised learning are effective, they are limited by the need for labelled data.  To address this challenge, researchers have developed unsupervised algorithms that can help to improve the performance of supervised models by identifying and exploiting underlying patterns in data.  A key area of focus for these algorithms is identifying features within data that are relevant to a specific task, a process known as feature learning.  To this end, researchers have proposed a new approach called Decomposed Inductive Method Learning (DIML), which is designed to learn the underlying structure of data and enable better generalisation performance.  By decomposing complex data into its constituent features, DIML enables the discovery of underlying patterns that can be used to improve model performance.  Importantly, the proposed approach can be applied to a wide range of data types, including image and text, without requiring significant amounts of labelled data.  Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of DIML, which outperforms existing methods on a variety of benchmark tasks.

The widespread presence of fabricated news has become a pressing concern, significantly influencing public opinion. This study tackles the issue of detecting English and Arabic fake news, focusing on non-essential alterations as a key factor. By leveraging automatic news creation, researchers gain a deeper understanding of fake news characteristics. This investigation delves into the implications of syntactic and syntagmatic text modifications on the creation of fake news, shedding light on the distinctions between altered and unaltered texts. The study also undertakes experiments to assess the influence of text alterations on the performance of fake news detection models. Furthermore, a new, state-of-the-art fake news classification system is developed, built on a large, manually curated dataset comprising over 50,000 Arabic and 10,000 English news articles. The study's contributions include this large dataset, a system capable of identifying Arabic fake news, and a framework for evaluating the effectiveness of text manipulation in detecting fake news, ultimately providing valuable insights for researchers and developers in this area.

The original proof provided no justification for the effective use of the modular forms' $q$-expansions' leading coefficients to determine the rank of the torsion groups. A corrected proof for this specific case can be found in [10], and it relies on a method by N. K. Horton and J. Park in [10] to bound the rational torsion.
